# Going to sea: who writes what down {#sec-at-sea}

::: {.callout-note}
**Written by AI, not yet reviewed by a person.** Drafted by Claude (Anthropic) on 2026-10-19 from the maintainer's
direction for the book's first chapter (fishycode plan 033 §4). The survey data are MFRI's, published on the
maintainer's web space and cleared by him for the book; the trawler's logbook is shown as background, in figures only.
Reviewed by: nobody yet.

```{r setup}
#| include: false
# quarto's R may start in a C locale, which prints a degree sign as <U+00B0>
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8"))
library(tidyverse)
library(duckdbfs)
library(ramb)
# quarto runs this file from docs/; R/paths.R resolves $FISHYDATA
source("../R/paths.R")

## The survey: MFRI's spring groundfish survey (SMB), March 2019 -------------------------------
stations <- read_csv(fd_raw("survey", "is_smb_stations.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(year == 2019)
catch <- read_csv(fd_raw("survey", "is_smb_biological.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  semi_join(stations, by = "id")
tows <- rb_read_example("trawlsurveytows") |> collect()
tows <- sf::st_sf(id = tows$id.lgs,
                  geometry = sf::st_as_sfc(structure(tows$geometry, class = "WKB"), crs = 4326))
track <- rb_read_example("trawlsurvey") |> collect()
coast <- map_data("world", region = "Iceland")

## The trawler: one of the two commercial trawlers on the survey, its 2019 logbook --------------
TRAWLER <- 1277
lb_trip <- open_dataset(fd_curated("logbook", "trip.parquet")) |>
  filter(vid == TRAWLER, year(T1) == 2019, is.na(twin) | twin != "duplicate")
lb_haul <- open_dataset(fd_curated("logbook", "station.parquet")) |>
  filter(is.na(twin) | twin != "duplicate") |>
  inner_join(lb_trip |> select(.tid, schema), by = c(".tid", "schema"))
lb_catch <- open_dataset(fd_curated("logbook", "catch.parquet")) |>
  inner_join(lb_haul |> select(.sid, schema, date), by = c(".sid", "schema"))
species <- open_dataset(fd_raw("oracle", "taxon", "species.parquet")) |>
  select(sid = species_no, species = eng_name) |> collect() |>
  mutate(species = str_to_lower(species))
trips <- lb_trip |> select(T1, T2) |> collect() |> arrange(T1)
hauls <- lb_haul |> select(.sid, date) |> collect()
hcatch <- lb_catch |> select(.sid, date, sid, catch) |> collect() |>
  left_join(species, by = "sid")

## Numbers used in the text --------------------------------------------------------------------
s_trawler <- stations |> filter(vid == TRAWLER)
n_tows <- nrow(stations)
n_tows_trawler <- nrow(s_trawler)
survey_days <- range(as_date(s_trawler$t1))
n_trips <- nrow(trips)
days_at_sea <- round(sum(as.numeric(difftime(trips$T2, trips$T1, units = "days"))))
n_hauls <- nrow(hauls)
tonnes <- round(sum(hcatch$catch, na.rm = TRUE) / 1000)
```

Two people can go to sea on the same boat in the same month and come home with different records. One is a
scientist, the other a fisher. Both write things down at sea, and both are careful. They are simply interested in
different things.

- **The scientist** wants to know what is in the sea. Every tow is made the same way at a station set in advance.
  Everything in the net is sorted, counted and weighed, and the depth, the temperature and the wind are noted.
- **The fisher** wants to know whether the trip paid. The haul goes where the fish are expected to be. The skipper
  estimates the catch in kilograms by species, as the logbook requires, and the sales note at the quay says what it
  was worth. The days at sea say what it cost.

This book is about what the second kind of record can tell the first kind of person: how a scientist gets a
quantitative view of a commercial fishery from records made for control and for selling fish. To see the gap, it
helps to watch both at work. Iceland offers a neat case: its spring groundfish survey is carried out partly by
commercial trawlers, chartered for three weeks in March.

## A scientist's day at sea

In March 2019 four vessels made `r n_tows` tows on the Icelandic spring groundfish survey (@fig-survey). Two were
research vessels. The other two were commercial trawlers, which for three weeks fished where the plan said rather than
where the fish were, and were paid for it. Each tow lasted about an hour and covered about four nautical miles.

```{r}
#| label: fig-survey
#| fig-cap: "The tows of the Icelandic spring groundfish survey, 27 February to 19 March 2019 (ramb's `trawlsurveytows`), with the cod caught in each (MFRI). Every tow is the same length, at a station fixed in advance, so differences in catch are differences in the sea."
#| fig-height: 5.5
cod <- catch |> filter(species == "cod") |> select(id, kg)
mid <- stations |> transmute(id, lon = (lon1 + lon2) / 2, lat = (lat1 + lat2) / 2) |>
  left_join(cod, by = "id") |> mutate(kg = replace_na(kg, 0))
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = coast, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = "grey85", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = tows, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = mid, aes(lon, lat, size = kg), shape = 21, fill = "#C0504D", alpha = 0.5, colour = "white") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, name = "cod, kg per tow") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-28, -10), ylim = c(62.8, 67.6)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

What one tow leaves behind is a small, tidy record (@tbl-tow). It holds the place, the time and the gear, plus the
conditions on the bottom. Then comes every species in the net, counted and weighed. The full survey also measures
lengths and takes otoliths for age; the public file used here keeps the counts and weights.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tow
#| tbl-cap: "One tow of the survey, as the scientist records it: the station, then the catch."
one <- 491031
st1 <- stations |> filter(id == one)
tibble(
  item = c("date", "start and end (UTC)", "start position", "depth (m)", "bottom temperature (\u00b0C)",
           "wind", "tow length (nautical miles)", "duration (min)"),
  value = c(format(st1$date), paste(format(st1$t1, "%H:%M"), "to", format(st1$t2, "%H:%M")),
            sprintf("%.3f\u00b0N %.3f\u00b0W", st1$lat1, -st1$lon1), st1$z1, st1$temp_b, st1$wind,
            st1$towlength, st1$duration)
) |> knitr::kable()
catch |> filter(id == one) |>
  transmute(species, number = n, kg = round(kg), `mean weight (g)` = round(1000 * kg / n)) |>
  arrange(desc(kg)) |> knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Seen from the vessel, the same day is a stream of positions, a ping about every ten minutes from the vessel's
tracking system, with the tows inside it (@fig-day). The track itself does not say when the net is down. The station record
does: the tows' start and end times mark which pings were fishing.

```{r}
#| label: fig-day
#| fig-cap: "One survey day of the trawler: its positions (ramb's `trawlsurvey`) and its tows. The pings come from the tracking system; whether the net was down comes from the station record."
#| fig-height: 5
day <- as_date(st1$t1)
d <- track |> filter(vid == TRAWLER, as_date(time) == day) |> arrange(time)
ggplot(d, aes(lon, lat)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = behaviour), size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(hauling = "#C0504D", "not hauling" = "grey50"), name = NULL) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## The same trawler, the rest of the year

From late March the trawler went back to work. In 2019 its logbook holds `r n_trips` trips, about `r days_at_sea` days
at sea and `r format(n_hauls, big.mark = ",")` hauls, with some `r format(tonnes, big.mark = ",")` tonnes of fish
(@fig-year). Its survey weeks sit inside that year, with a few short commercial trips between the survey's legs.
None of those hauls is at a survey station: the two records stay apart.

```{r}
#| label: fig-year
#| fig-cap: "The trawler's 2019: each logbook trip from departure to return, and its survey weeks (shaded). The logbook trip is what the control and the sale need: when the vessel left, when it came back, and what it caught."
#| fig-height: 2.2
ggplot(trips) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = as_datetime(survey_days[1]), xmax = as_datetime(survey_days[2] + 1),
           ymin = 0, ymax = 1, fill = "#C0504D", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = T1, xmax = T2 + days(1), ymin = 0.2, ymax = 0.8), fill = "grey40") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%b") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

What the fisher writes down is the haul and the catch in kilograms by species. There is no count of fish, no
length and no bottom temperature, because the logbook is a declaration, not a survey. Over the year it adds up to a
picture the scientist cannot get from a survey: where and when the fleet actually fishes, and how much (@fig-month).

```{r}
#| label: fig-month
#| fig-cap: "The trawler's logbook catch by month and species, 2019, in tonnes, as the skipper declared it."
#| fig-height: 3.5
top <- hcatch |> count(species, wt = catch, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 5) |> pull(species)
hcatch |>
  mutate(species = if_else(species %in% top, species, "other"),
         month = month(date, label = TRUE)) |>
  count(month, species, wt = catch / 1000, name = "tonnes") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, tonnes, fill = species)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "tonnes") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The two records also catch fish differently (@fig-compare). A survey tow is an hour at a fixed station: it catches
whatever is there, often little. A commercial haul goes where the skipper expects fish, for as long as it pays, so
its catch of cod is typically many times larger. Neither is wrong. They answer different questions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare
#| fig-cap: "Cod per tow on the survey and per haul in the logbook, for the same trawler in 2019 (tows and hauls with cod). The survey samples the sea; the fishery samples where the fish are."
#| fig-height: 3
bind_rows(
  catch |> filter(species == "cod") |> semi_join(s_trawler, by = "id") |>
    transmute(record = "survey tow (scientist)", kg),
  hcatch |> filter(sid == 1, catch > 0) |> transmute(record = "logbook haul (fisher)", kg = catch)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(kg, fill = record)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5, colour = NA) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("survey tow (scientist)" = "#C0504D", "logbook haul (fisher)" = "grey40"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "cod, kg (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

And the money? The scientist's record has none. The fisher's sits in two other places: the sales note at landing,
which gives the value, and the days at sea, which drive the cost in fuel and crew. Neither is in the files used here.
Iceland's sales notes carry the weight, and the value is not in this extract. That is a fair summary of the
situation the rest of this book works in: the records that matter to the fisher are rarely the ones that reach the
scientist whole.

## One grammar for both

Survey and logbook look different, but they share a shape: a trip holds stations, a station holds what was caught,
and the vessel's positions run alongside as a separate stream. The working groups describe the same shape. A trip
runs from leaving port to returning, with fishing in between. A fishing event is a haul, or a use of passive gear, as
the logbook holds it (WKSSFGEO 2022, pp. 13-14). A logbook trip holds log events, each with the species landed, and
a new event starts with each change of gear or area (WGSFD 2025a, p. 34). How fine those events are differs between
countries and fleets. Some records give each haul with its times. Others give a day in a rectangle. Many small-scale
fleets give only a landing date and place (WGSFD 2025a, pp. 12-13).

| Level | The scientist's record | The fisher's record |
|---|---|---|
| Trip | the survey leg | the fishing trip, from departure to landing |
| Station | the tow: start and end, position, depth, temperature, wind | the haul: date and position, the time where recorded |
| Sample | the gear, and the whole catch sorted | the gear |
| Observation | each species counted, weighed, measured | each species' catch, estimated in kilograms |
| Streams alongside | the vessel's positions | the vessel's positions; the landings (sales notes) |

This book calls that shape a grammar: trip, station, sample and observation, with pings and landings as parallel
streams. The full grammar, with every level's fields, is in [the appendix](grammar.qmd). Here it is enough that both
records fit it, and that each fills it in its own way.

The next chapter takes the scientist's side of the gap. What can be known about a commercial fishery from records like
the fisher's, and from the positions running alongside them? What happens when even those are missing, as they are
for most small boats?
